Intel (INTC) shares climbed 2.86% to $56.03 at 10:35 a.m. ET on Friday, November 27, as chip shares rebounded, even as court filings shed new light on how Washington became a major holder. Documents in a Delaware shareholder lawsuit, first reported by WIRED, show the Commerce Department pressed Intel to hand over about 10% of its equity in exchange for releasing $8.9 billion in grants the company had already won.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 2 Warning Sign with PLTR.

Is PLTR fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

A CHIPS Program Office lawyer told Intel's finance chief in August 2025 not to make the "mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation," according to The Next Web's account of the filings. Board minutes described the terms as unattractive in their original form. Intel's motion to dismiss argues the board did negotiate and secured immediate release of the grants, and a hearing is set for December 10. Kantan News put the stake at roughly 275 million shares.

The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 70/100, with a decent balance sheet and very strong momentum, but valuation is the weak link. The GF Value of $34.09 sits far below the share price, putting Intel at a 64.4% premium that GuruFocus labels significantly overvalued. At $56.03, 275 million shares are worth about $15.4 billion, well above the $8.9 billion in grants exchanged, a gap the plaintiffs could frame as value shifted away from other holders. The next test is the December 10 hearing on the motions to dismiss.

A trader spent weeks testing more than 100 trading strategies and roughly 700 variations, hoping to find approaches that could consistently beat the stock market. With the help of AI, they built a Python program to test everything from chart patterns and insider buying to machine learning models and AI-powered stock predictions.

The results weren't encouraging. Most strategies failed once real trading costs and other factors were included. And the trader found the reasons behind those failures more useful than the handful of strategies that appeared to work.

AI Can Write The Code. But Can It Understand The Code? This Startup Is Building The Missing Layer.

Teachers, Nurses And First Responders Are Being Priced Out Of The Communities They Serve. That's putting a different part of the housing market in the spotlight.

"Most of it didn't survive," the trader wrote on Reddit's r/algotrading forum recently. "Writing this up because the reasons they died were more useful to me than the few that worked."

Why So Many Strategies Failed

One of the biggest surprises was how little a high win rate actually meant. A strategy that bought the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), an exchange-traded fund tracking the S&P 500, won 69% of its trades but returned just 16.9% over 10 years. Simply holding SPY during that period would have returned 214.9%.

Trading costs were another problem. One machine learning model appeared to beat its group of stocks by 13.2% annually before costs. But when trading costs increased, that advantage dropped to just 2.4%.

Even popular chart patterns struggled. Several setups performed no better than buying stocks at random, despite producing what looked like promising results.

title: How Much More Could You Lose In Intel Stock?
detail:
How Much More Could You Lose In Intel Stock?
Trefis Team
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 3:59 AM PST 4 min read
INTC
^GSPC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Anthropic Broke Its $83 IPO Price. What Did Facebook Do Next?

Intel stock closed at $54.47 on Wednesday, 61.4% below its highest close of the past year, $140.94 on June 22. Its worst day was October 30, a 28.6% drop right after its quarterly report. After a fall that size, the damage can look done. So if the whole market turns, how much more could an Intel owner lose?

How far did Intel fall when the market turned?

The slide since June is not one of the market-wide sell-offs in our record, so a market shock would come on top of it. In 15 such shocks since 2007, the deepest fall came in the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis. Intel lost 54%, about as much as the S&P 500's 53%. The January to October 2022 sell-off hit Intel harder, a 52% fall against 24% for the index. Across all 15 shocks, Intel fell 22.9% on average, against 15.8% for the S&P 500.

Getting back could be slow. Half the recoveries took 5 months or less, but five of the 15 took more than a year. After its October 2022 low, Intel needed 39.4 months to climb back to its January 2022 peak close.

Intel took 39.4 months to climb back after its October 2022 low, and today it returns no cash to owners while they wait. If that money has to cover your living costs, a wait that long means nothing coming in, or selling shares near the bottom. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

How does Intel's business look today?

Sales are growing again. Revenue over the past year was $59.9 billion, up 12.1%. Growth slowed to 20.9% in the quarter ended September, from 25.4% in the June quarter. The operating margin over the past year was 10.1%. That is up from a slight loss a year earlier, but far below its ten-year peak of 33.6%.

The balance sheet is stronger, partly because Intel sold $23 billion of new shares in August 2026. At the end of September, it held $54 billion of cash and short-term investments against $50.1 billion of debt. Its diluted share count rose to 5,307 million from 4,531 million a year earlier.

What is getting worse at Intel now?

PC chips are the main worry. On its October 29 call, management said it expected industry-wide PC unit sales to fall about 12% in 2026. It was planning for roughly 10% fewer in 2027 and did not expect a sustained recovery until memory supply and prices improve. It expected client revenue, $8.1 billion in the September quarter, to drop more than 20% in the December quarter. Data center revenue, by contrast, was expected to grow by a mid-teens percentage from the September quarter.

Why Is Intel Stock Rallying Today?

Intel logo on building ©Shutterstock

Shares of Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) rose 4.5% to approximately $56.91 in pre-market trading on Friday, supported by a broader semiconductor sector recovery and recent progress in the company's contract chip manufacturing business.

The rebound follows a volatile previous trading session, during which Intel shares fell to an intraday low of $49.16 before recovering to close at $54.47.

How Is Intel's Foundry Business Supporting Its Share Price?

Intel recently announced that it had secured its first external customer for its advanced 18A semiconductor manufacturing technology.

Speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas, on 18 November, Chief Executive Officer Lip-Bu Tan said: "And then 18A, I'm involved in production and we just signed the first customer."

Tan also indicated that the manufacturing yield for Intel's 18A technology had reached 70%.

Separately, Microsoft became the first company to publicly announce plans to use Intel Foundry's EMIB advanced packaging technology for its own Azure semiconductors.

These developments represent progress in Intel's efforts to expand its third-party semiconductor manufacturing business.

What Is Wall Street's Current Outlook for Intel?

Analyst sentiment towards Intel remains mixed despite recent progress in its foundry operations.

Sanford C. Bernstein downgraded Intel from Strong Buy to Hold on 25 November, while Zacks Research assigned the stock a Hold rating on 26 November.

The broader analyst consensus stands at Hold, with an average price target of $96.93.

Meanwhile, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan purchased 150,000 shares in early November at an average price of $64.73 per share, representing a transaction worth approximately $9.7 million.

How Is the Broader Semiconductor Recovery Supporting Intel?

Intel's advance coincided with improving sentiment across US equity markets, with the Nasdaq gaining 2.4% and the S&P 500 rising 1.8%.

Semiconductor shares have experienced considerable selling pressure in recent weeks, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index declining sharply from its previous peak.

Friday's recovery follows the Thanksgiving holiday, with US equity markets operating a shortened Black Friday trading session.

From a technical perspective, Intel shares have recovered above the closely watched $50 level following several periods of selling pressure.

What Risks Does Intel Continue to Face?

Despite the recent recovery, Intel continues to face legal uncertainty associated with securities class action lawsuits concerning allegations of misleading statements about challenges in the personal computer market between July and October 2026.

The outcome and potential financial implications of these proceedings remain uncertain.

Investors continue to monitor Intel's progress in attracting external manufacturing customers, expanding its advanced packaging business and addressing challenges across its existing operations.
